title: Python: How Code Becomes State
question: What actually changes when Python executes one line?
intuition: Python evaluates expressions, binds names to objects, changes program state, and produces observable output. Thinking in state changes is more reliable than memorising syntax.
technical: Execution is a sequence of evaluation, name binding, function calls and control-flow decisions. Types define available operations; mutability determines whether an object can change in place.
practitioner: Trace variables and types at each meaningful step. When debugging, ask which assumption about state stopped being true.
breakPrompt: Change an input type and predict which operation will fail first.

title: Functions & Reusable Reasoning
question: Why do functions make programs easier to trust?
intuition: A function packages one transformation behind a clear interface: inputs enter, a result or side effect leaves, and the implementation can be tested independently.
technical: Function parameters create local bindings; return values communicate results. Pure functions minimise hidden state, while side-effecting functions should make their effects explicit.
practitioner: Prefer small functions with one responsibility, descriptive names, explicit inputs and testable outputs.
breakPrompt: Add hidden global state, then observe why the same call can stop producing the same result.

title: Choosing Python Collections
question: List, tuple, set or dictionary—what changes when you choose the wrong one?
intuition: Collections encode assumptions about order, uniqueness, mutability and lookup. The right data structure makes intended operations obvious and accidental complexity harder.
technical: Lists provide ordered mutable sequences; tuples are ordered and immutable; sets optimise uniqueness/membership; dictionaries map keys to values with fast key-based lookup.
practitioner: Choose by operations, not habit. If identity matters, use keys; if uniqueness matters, use sets; if order and repetition matter, use sequences.
breakPrompt: Replace a dictionary lookup with repeated list scanning and compare the mental and computational cost.

title: pandas & Table Thinking
question: What does a DataFrame represent beyond “an Excel-like table”?
intuition: A DataFrame is a labelled, typed table where rows have a grain and columns have meanings. Good pandas work starts by preserving those semantics through each transformation.
technical: Selection, filtering, grouping, joining and reshaping transform table structure. Index alignment and data types can silently affect results, so intermediate inspection matters.
practitioner: State row grain before merging or aggregating. Inspect shape, dtypes, keys and missingness after major transformations.
breakPrompt: Create a many-to-many merge accidentally and watch row counts explode.

title: SQL Query Flow
question: How does SQL turn tables into evidence?
intuition: SQL declares the result you want; the database engine determines an execution plan. The learner’s job is to reason about row grain, filters, joins and aggregation.
technical: Logical query processing can be reasoned about as FROM/JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY, even though the optimiser may execute differently.
practitioner: Validate join cardinality and aggregation grain. A syntactically correct query can still answer the wrong business question.
breakPrompt: Change an inner join to a left join and predict which entities reappear.

title: Excel as an Analytical Model
question: When is a spreadsheet a model rather than just a grid?
intuition: A spreadsheet becomes an analytical model when data, assumptions, formulas and outputs are organised so another person can trace how a result was produced.
technical: Cell references form a dependency graph. Tables, named ranges, structured references, PivotTables and Power Query reduce fragile manual steps.
practitioner: Separate raw data, transformation logic and outputs. Avoid hard-coded constants inside formulas when they represent assumptions.
breakPrompt: Insert a row into a fragile range and compare it with a structured-table formula.

title: Missing Data Decisions
question: A blank cell is not a method—what should you decide before imputing?
intuition: Missingness has a cause. Deletion, simple imputation, local imputation or model-native handling can each be reasonable, but only when their assumptions match how values became missing.
technical: MCAR, MAR and MNAR describe relationships between missingness and observed/unobserved values. Imputation parameters must be learned inside training folds to avoid leakage.
practitioner: Profile missingness by feature, subgroup and time. Compare strategies on downstream validation and inspect post-imputation distributions.
breakPrompt: Impute before splitting the data and identify where information from the test set leaks backward.

title: Scaling & Distance
question: Why can a harmless-looking unit change alter a model?
intuition: Distance- and gradient-based methods react to numerical scale. Changing kilometres to metres should not make one feature semantically more important, yet raw magnitudes can do exactly that.
technical: Standardisation centres and rescales by training mean/std; Min–Max scaling maps a range; robust scaling uses resistant statistics. Tree splits generally do not require scaling.
practitioner: Fit scaling only on training data and include it inside a pipeline. Inspect transformed distributions and remember that scaling does not fix outliers or skew by itself.
breakPrompt: Multiply one feature by 1,000 and watch KNN/SVM geometry change before and after scaling.

title: Categorical Encoding
question: How do categories become numbers without inventing false meaning?
intuition: Models need numerical representations, but the encoding determines what relationships the model can infer. One-hot preserves nominal identity; ordinal encoding intentionally imposes order.
technical: One-hot creates indicator columns; ordinal maps ordered levels; target encoding uses outcome statistics and therefore requires strict out-of-fold handling.
practitioner: Choose encoding from semantics and model family. Never let target-derived encodings see validation labels.
breakPrompt: Assign arbitrary integers to unordered cities and observe the artificial order you created.

title: Exploratory Data Analysis
question: What should you learn before fitting a model?
intuition: EDA is disciplined interrogation of the dataset: structure, distributions, relationships, missingness, anomalies and potential data-generating processes.
technical: Univariate summaries reveal centre/spread; bivariate views reveal association; multivariate analysis surfaces interactions and confounding. EDA must respect future validation boundaries when it influences modelling decisions.
practitioner: Ask a question before making a plot. Record observations, hypotheses and decisions instead of producing charts without interpretation.
breakPrompt: Hide an outlier or subgroup and see how a single aggregate can tell a different story.

title: Visualisation & Storytelling
question: What makes a chart explain rather than decorate?
intuition: A chart is an encoding of evidence. Good visualisation chooses position, length, colour and annotation to make the intended comparison effortless and honest.
technical: Chart selection follows the analytical task: comparison, trend, distribution, relationship, composition or uncertainty. Axis scales and aggregation choices can distort perception.
practitioner: Write the takeaway first, then choose the simplest encoding that supports it. Label units, show uncertainty when relevant and remove non-informative decoration.
breakPrompt: Truncate an axis or switch aggregation and inspect how the apparent story changes.

title: Train, Validation & Test
question: Why do we need data the model has never seen?
intuition: Training measures fit; validation guides choices; testing estimates final generalisation. Mixing these roles lets decisions adapt to the answer key.
technical: Repeated model selection on a validation set gradually overfits that validation evidence. The final test set should remain untouched until choices are frozen.
practitioner: Split by the deployment unit—person, customer, device, time—not blindly by row.
breakPrompt: Tune repeatedly on the test set and watch the “final” estimate stop being independent.

title: Cross-Validation
question: How do we estimate generalisation when one split is too fragile?
intuition: Cross-validation rotates which observations are held out, giving several views of model performance and revealing variability that one split can hide.
technical: K-Fold assumes exchangeable independent observations; stratification preserves class proportions; grouped CV keeps related entities together; time-series CV preserves temporal order.
practitioner: Choose the split strategy from the data-generating process, not from habit. Report fold variability as well as the mean.
breakPrompt: Use ordinary K-Fold on repeated measurements from the same person and locate the leakage path.

title: Data Leakage
question: Can a model look excellent because we accidentally gave it the answer?
intuition: Leakage occurs when training uses information that would not be available at prediction time or information from held-out data. It often produces impressive but unreproducible performance.
technical: Leakage can enter through preprocessing, target proxies, duplicates, grouped entities, temporal look-ahead or feature engineering performed before splitting.
practitioner: Build transformations inside pipelines and audit every feature with one question: “Would I know this value at the moment of prediction?”
breakPrompt: Fit preprocessing on the entire dataset, then compare the inflated validation score with a leakage-safe pipeline.

title: Linear Regression
question: What does “best-fitting line” really optimise?
intuition: Linear regression learns coefficients that make predicted values close to observed targets under a squared-error objective. Coefficients quantify conditional linear associations.
technical: OLS minimises the sum of squared residuals. Matrix form gives β̂=(XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy when conditions permit; regularised variants change the objective to stabilise estimates.
practitioner: Inspect residuals, nonlinearity, influential points and extrapolation. Coefficients are not automatically causal effects.
breakPrompt: Add one extreme outlier and watch squared error pull the fitted line toward it.

title: Logistic Regression
question: How does a linear model become a probability classifier?
intuition: Logistic regression learns a linear score and maps it through the logistic function, producing a probability that can be thresholded into a class decision.
technical: The model is linear in log-odds. Training minimises log loss; regularisation controls coefficient magnitude. The decision boundary is linear unless features are transformed.
practitioner: Use it as a strong interpretable baseline. Check calibration, class imbalance, multicollinearity and nonlinear patterns.
breakPrompt: Move the classification threshold without retraining and watch precision/recall trade places.

title: Decision Trees
question: How does a tree convert questions into regions of feature space?
intuition: A decision tree recursively asks threshold questions that make child groups more homogeneous. Each path is an explicit rule from root to leaf.
technical: Classification trees optimise impurity reduction; regression trees reduce squared error or related criteria. Depth/min-samples constraints regulate variance.
practitioner: Trees are interpretable but unstable. Use pruning/regularisation and compare with ensembles when predictive stability matters.
breakPrompt: Increase maximum depth until training error collapses while validation error worsens.

title: Random Forest
question: Why can many unstable trees become a stable model?
intuition: Random Forest builds many deliberately different trees and averages/votes their predictions. Diversity reduces the variance that makes a single deep tree unstable.
technical: Bootstrap sampling varies training rows; random feature subsets decorrelate tree structures. Averaging reduces variance most when individual errors are not perfectly correlated.
practitioner: Strong default for tabular data. Tune tree size/depth/features, inspect OOB or CV performance, and treat impurity importance cautiously.
breakPrompt: Increase tree correlation by removing feature randomness and observe why averaging helps less.

title: Gradient Boosting
question: How can a sequence of weak models repair its own mistakes?
intuition: Boosting adds learners sequentially. Each new learner focuses on the residual error or gradient left by the current ensemble.
technical: Gradient boosting performs stage-wise functional optimisation. Learning rate controls step size; tree depth controls interaction complexity; early stopping regulates overfit.
practitioner: Use careful validation and monitor training rounds. Lower learning rates often require more trees.
breakPrompt: Set learning rate very high and watch the ensemble overshoot useful corrections.

title: K-Nearest Neighbours
question: What happens when prediction is literally “look at similar examples”?
intuition: KNN stores training examples and predicts from the labels or targets of nearby points. The geometry of the feature space is therefore the model.
technical: Distance metric, scaling, k and weighting define neighbourhoods. Small k lowers bias but raises variance; large k smooths local structure.
practitioner: Scale features and consider dimensionality. KNN can be expensive at inference and deteriorates in high-dimensional sparse spaces.
breakPrompt: Move k from 1 to a large value and watch local boundaries become smoother.

title: Support Vector Machines
question: Why do only a few boundary points determine the classifier?
intuition: An SVM chooses a separating boundary with a wide margin. Points touching or violating the margin—the support vectors—determine the solution.
technical: Soft-margin SVM balances margin width and violations through C. Kernels replace dot products to create nonlinear boundaries in an implicit feature space.
practitioner: Scale inputs. Tune C and kernel parameters jointly. Probability estimates require additional calibration.
breakPrompt: Increase C and watch the model trade a wider margin for fewer training errors.

title: K-Means Clustering
question: How do unlabeled points organise themselves around centroids?
intuition: K-Means alternates between assigning each point to its nearest centroid and moving each centroid to the mean of its assigned points.
technical: The algorithm optimises within-cluster sum of squares but can converge to local minima. k-means++ improves initialisation. Euclidean spherical-cluster assumptions matter.
practitioner: Scale features, try multiple initialisations, and validate whether clusters are useful—not merely compact.
breakPrompt: Change k and initial centroids to see different local solutions on the same data.

title: Principal Component Analysis
question: How can we rotate a feature space without throwing away its main variation?
intuition: PCA finds orthogonal directions that capture as much variance as possible, then represents observations using coordinates along those directions.
technical: Eigenvectors of the covariance matrix (or SVD of centred data) define principal directions. Components are ordered by explained variance.
practitioner: Scale features when units differ meaningfully. PCA maximises variance, not task relevance or interpretability.
breakPrompt: Rescale one feature and watch the first principal direction rotate toward it.

title: Classification Metrics
question: Why can “90% accuracy” be terrible?
intuition: Metrics encode which mistakes matter. Accuracy treats all correct decisions equally; precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC, PR-AUC and log loss answer different questions.
technical: Confusion-matrix counts produce threshold-dependent metrics. Ranking metrics evaluate score ordering; probabilistic metrics evaluate probability quality.
practitioner: Start from decision costs and class prevalence. For rare positives, PR curves and precision/recall are often more informative than accuracy.
breakPrompt: Make positives rare while keeping accuracy high and inspect what the confusion matrix reveals.

title: Regression Metrics & Residuals
question: What does one error number hide?
intuition: MAE, RMSE and R² summarise different aspects of prediction error. Residual plots reveal structure that a single scalar cannot.
technical: MAE weights errors linearly; MSE/RMSE square errors; R² compares residual variation with a mean baseline. Heteroscedasticity and systematic residual patterns indicate model mismatch.
practitioner: Report a metric that matches business cost, plus residual diagnostics and subgroup performance.
breakPrompt: Add a few large errors and compare how MAE and RMSE respond.

title: Bias, Variance & Learning Curves
question: Is poor validation performance caused by underfitting or instability?
intuition: Bias describes systematic simplification; variance describes sensitivity to training data. Learning curves compare training and validation performance as data grows.
technical: High bias often yields similarly poor train/validation scores; high variance yields a large gap. Regularisation, data size and model complexity move the trade-off.
practitioner: Diagnose before tuning. More complexity does not solve high variance; more data does not always solve high bias.
breakPrompt: Increase model complexity and watch training error fall before validation error eventually rises.

title: Regularisation
question: How do we tell a flexible model not to chase every detail?
intuition: Regularisation penalises or constrains complexity so the fitted model prefers simpler solutions unless extra complexity clearly improves the objective.
technical: L2 shrinks coefficients smoothly; L1 can drive some to zero; early stopping limits optimisation time; dropout regularises neural networks stochastically.
practitioner: Tune regularisation inside validation. Standardise features before coefficient penalties when scales differ.
breakPrompt: Increase λ and watch coefficients shrink while bias rises and variance falls.

title: Hyperparameter Optimisation
question: How do we search a large configuration space without fooling ourselves?
intuition: HPO treats validation performance as an objective over configuration choices such as depth, learning rate or regularisation.
technical: Grid search enumerates a lattice; random search samples dimensions efficiently; Bayesian/TPE methods use previous trials; Hyperband allocates budget adaptively.
practitioner: Define a sensible search space and validation design first. More trials cannot rescue a leaky or noisy objective.
breakPrompt: Search a parameter that barely matters and see how grid search wastes budget compared with random search.

title: Probability Calibration & Thresholds
question: Is a predicted 0.8 probability actually an 80% event rate?
intuition: Discrimination asks whether positives rank above negatives; calibration asks whether predicted probabilities match observed frequencies. Thresholding then turns probabilities into decisions.
technical: Reliability diagrams and Brier/log loss assess calibration. Platt, isotonic and temperature scaling transform scores using separate calibration evidence.
practitioner: Separate model fitting, calibration and threshold choice. Choose thresholds from decision costs, not the default 0.5 by reflex.
breakPrompt: Hold ranking fixed but distort probabilities, then compare AUC with calibration error.

title: Explainability & Model Interpretation
question: How do statistical significance, feature AUC, model importance and RFE answer different questions?
intuition: Feature evidence can come from statistical significance, single-feature discrimination, model reliance, subset selection or local prediction effects. These are related but not interchangeable.
technical: Welch t-tests produce p-values for class-mean differences; univariate ROC-AUC measures ranking discrimination; permutation importance measures held-out performance loss; RFE recursively removes weak model features; local methods explain individual predictions.
practitioner: Use multiple evidence types, keep selection inside training/validation data, account for multiple testing where appropriate, and never equate importance with causality.
breakPrompt: Duplicate a correlated feature and observe how importance can split or move between substitutes.

title: Predictive Uncertainty
question: When should a model say “I am not sure”?
intuition: Point predictions hide uncertainty from noise, limited data and model uncertainty. Intervals or predictive distributions make that uncertainty visible.
technical: Aleatoric uncertainty comes from irreducible outcome variation; epistemic uncertainty reflects limited knowledge. Conformal methods can provide coverage guarantees under assumptions.
practitioner: Evaluate interval coverage and width, not only point error. Escalate or abstain when uncertainty is operationally important.
breakPrompt: Move a test point far outside the training region and compare point prediction confidence with uncertainty.

title: Time-Series Forecasting
question: Why can’t time-ordered data be shuffled like ordinary rows?
intuition: Forecasting predicts the future from information available in the past. Temporal order creates dependence, trend, seasonality and a strict information boundary.
technical: Lag features, differencing, autoregression and state-space/decomposition methods model temporal structure. Validation must roll forward rather than sample future observations into training.
practitioner: Always define forecast horizon and prediction origin. Compare against naive seasonal baselines.
breakPrompt: Randomly split a time series and identify how future patterns leak into training.

title: Neural Networks & Backpropagation
question: How does a network turn many simple transformations into complex behaviour?
intuition: A neural network composes affine transformations and nonlinear activations. Training adjusts weights so the final outputs reduce a loss function.
technical: Backpropagation applies the chain rule to compute gradients efficiently through the computational graph; an optimiser uses those gradients to update parameters.
practitioner: Monitor training/validation curves, scale inputs, tune learning rate carefully and use regularisation/normalisation where appropriate.
breakPrompt: Increase learning rate until loss oscillates or diverges.

title: Attention & Transformers
question: How can each token decide which other tokens matter?
intuition: Attention computes content-dependent weights between elements, allowing each token to combine information from relevant context rather than relying only on fixed local recurrence.
technical: Scaled dot-product attention uses softmax(QKᵀ/√d)V. Multi-head attention learns multiple relation subspaces; positional information restores order.
practitioner: Inspect sequence length/memory costs and remember attention weights are not automatically causal explanations.
breakPrompt: Increase attention sharpness and watch one context token dominate the representation.

title: Graph Neural Networks
question: How can information move across relationships rather than rows?
intuition: GNNs update each node by combining its own representation with messages from neighbours. Repeating layers expands the receptive field through the graph.
technical: Message passing defines message, aggregation and update functions. GCN normalises neighbour aggregation; GAT learns attention weights; GIN uses expressive sum aggregation plus an MLP.
practitioner: Match graph construction to the real relational process. Too many layers can oversmooth node representations.
breakPrompt: Add more message-passing layers and observe when node representations become too similar.

title: Deployment, Drift & Monitoring
question: What changes after a model leaves the notebook?
intuition: Production models interact with changing data, systems and decisions. Monitoring asks whether inputs, predictions, calibration and outcomes still resemble the evidence used to validate the model.
technical: Data drift changes input distributions; concept drift changes P(y|x); performance drift is observed degradation. Detection requires reference windows, delayed labels and response policies.
practitioner: Define thresholds and owners before deployment. Retraining should be governed, reproducible and evaluated against the current champion.
breakPrompt: Shift an input distribution without changing labels, then distinguish data drift from concept drift.
